unit.name: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter

chapter: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter
question_text: Describe an experiment to study the effect of frequency of incident radiation on 'stopping potential'.

verification.note: From FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students, physics section, Ch.12 (printed pp.43-44). The book prints no exam-year citations for this chapter. The 1+2+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Paper-II bank the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked physically: at constant intensity the stopping potential grows with frequency (V₀₂ > V₀₁ for ν₂ > ν₁); the V₀ against ν graph is a straight line obeying eV₀ = h(ν − ν₀), so its slope is h/e and its intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold frequency ν₀, below which no photoelectrons are emitted — the standard NCERT account and the basis of Millikan's determination of h. This is LAQ-grade material in most other syllabuses; it is kept as the 4-mark SAQ this book prints.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter · 4 marks

steps.label: The arrangement
lines: An evacuated glass tube has a photosensitive
cathode C and a metal anode A. Light of a
chosen frequency falls on the cathode C.
A battery and a rheostat set the potential of
the anode, which can be made positive or
negative with respect to C, and a
microammeter reads the photoelectric current.
steps.margin_note: One mark. Four parts to name: the evacuated tube, the two electrodes C and A, the variable potential, the microammeter.
steps.why: Each part has a job: the tube keeps the electron path clear, C emits, A collects, the battery and rheostat give the variable retarding potential, and the microammeter shows when the current reaches zero.
common_mistakes: Leaving out evacuated. In air the photoelectrons would collide with gas molecules before reaching the anode.
Leaving the potential fixed. The experiment needs the anode potential to be varied through negative values.

recall.must_convey: That an evacuated tube holds cathode C and anode A, the anode potential is varied by a battery and rheostat, and a microammeter reads the current.
accept: evacuated tube with cathode and anode
battery and rheostat vary the potential
reject: stopping potential is more for higher frequency

steps.memory_tip: Tube, C and A, a knob for the potential, a meter for the current — four parts, one sentence each.

steps.label: The circuit
steps.margin_note: Draw the tube with C and A inside, the light arrow onto C, the microammeter in the wire, and the battery with the rheostat below.
steps.why: The circuit is what makes 'vary the potential' concrete: the battery and rheostat sit in the loop, and the microammeter is in series so it reads the tube current directly.
common_mistakes: Putting the light on the anode. The light must fall on the photosensitive cathode C.
Leaving out the microammeter. Without it there is no way to see the current reach zero.

recall.must_convey: That the diagram shows the evacuated tube with C and A, light on C, a microammeter, and a battery with a rheostat.
accept: tube with cathode and anode and meter

steps.memory_tip: Light in at the top left, meter on the right, battery and rheostat along the bottom.

steps.label: Observations
lines: Keep the intensity of the light the same and
repeat the experiment with radiation of
different frequencies. For each frequency,
study how the photoelectric current changes
with the anode potential and note the
stopping potential where the current is zero.
The stopping potential is different for
different frequencies of the radiation.
For a higher frequency the stopping potential
is larger: V₀₂ > V₀₁ when ν₂ > ν₁. So the
maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons
depends only on the frequency, and not on
the intensity, of the incident radiation.
steps.margin_note: Two marks. The procedure (same intensity, different frequencies) and the finding: a higher frequency needs a larger stopping potential.
steps.why: The stopping potential measures the maximum kinetic energy through eV₀. A higher frequency photon carries more energy, so the fastest electrons need a stronger retarding potential to be stopped.
common_mistakes: Changing the intensity between readings. The intensity must be kept the same so only the frequency varies.
Saying the saturation current changes with frequency. It depends on the intensity, not the frequency.

recall.must_convey: That with intensity fixed, a higher frequency gives a larger stopping potential — V naught two greater than V naught one for nu two greater than nu one.
accept: higher frequency gives larger stopping potential
reject: slope of the line is h by e

steps.memory_tip: Fix the intensity, walk the frequency up, and watch V₀ walk up with it.

steps.label: Stopping potential against frequency
steps.margin_note: A straight line AB starting on the frequency axis at ν₀ — not at the origin.
steps.why: The line meets the axis at ν₀, not at O: radiation below the threshold frequency gives no photoelectrons, so there is no stopping potential to plot there.
common_mistakes: Starting the line at the origin. It starts at ν₀ on the frequency axis.
Curving the line. eV₀ = h(ν − ν₀) is linear in ν, so the graph is straight.

recall.must_convey: That the graph is a straight line AB meeting the frequency axis at the threshold frequency ν₀.
reject: three curves with one stopping potential

steps.memory_tip: The line starts on the frequency axis at ν₀ and climbs to the right.

steps.label: Slope h/e and threshold frequency
lines: The graph of V₀ against the frequency ν is a
straight line AB, obeying
The slope of the line is h/e, and the line
meets the frequency axis at the threshold
frequency ν₀. For radiation below ν₀ no
photoelectrons are emitted at any intensity.

lines.text: Slope = h/e, intercept on the ν-axis = ν₀

steps.margin_note: One mark. Read two numbers off the line: the slope h/e and the intercept ν₀.
steps.why: Einstein's equation eV₀ = hν − W₀ is the equation of this line, with W₀ = hν₀. Millikan measured the slope, multiplied by e, and obtained Planck's constant h — which is how the line verified the equation.
common_mistakes: Calling the slope h. The slope is h/e; multiplying by the electron charge gives h.
Reading the intercept as the work function. The intercept on the frequency axis is ν₀; the work function is W₀ = hν₀.

recall.must_convey: That the line's slope is h by e and its intercept on the frequency axis is the threshold frequency, below which no electrons are emitted.
reject: higher frequency gives larger stopping potential

steps.memory_tip: One line, two readings: slope h/e, intercept ν₀.

insider_note: Millikan used exactly this straight line — its slope times e gave Planck's constant. Name both the slope h/e and the intercept ν₀; one without the other reads as half the conclusion.
